segments.caption: Wellington. 128, off 153 balls.
Rishabh Pant's ninth Test hundred, and his first in New Zealand.
He's now the first Asian wicketkeeper with Test hundreds in all four SENA countries. And only Ben Stokes has hit more Test sixes.
53 Tests. 3,853 runs, at an average of almost 45.
Every bar is one innings. The line is his average over the last ten. It has never been a calm ride.
He got off the mark in Test cricket with a six.
A hundred at the Oval in only his third Test. 159 not out at Sydney.
And at the Gabba, 89 not out, to beat Australia at a ground where they hadn't lost in 32 years.
The lows were just as steep. In 2020, he averaged under 18.
Then, on 30 December 2022, a car crash nearly ended everything.
637 days later, in his first Test back, he made a hundred at Chennai.
At Leeds in 2025, he made a hundred in each innings. The only keeper to do that before him was Andy Flower.
Weeks later at Manchester, he walked out with a fractured foot, and made 54.
Now, the spin story.
Against pace, he averages 39. Against spin, 53, at 86 runs per 100 balls.
75 of his first 100 Test sixes came off spinners. And at home, against spin, he scores at almost a run a ball.
Nathan Lyon has dismissed him more than anyone, six times. But Pant has taken 258 runs, and seven sixes, off him.
Overseas, compare him with the leading keepers of the last two decades.
Pant has the best average away from home, almost 43, and the most away hundreds, seven.
And nobody here scores faster.
But there's one thing he still hasn't solved.
Seven times, he's been out in the nineties. Nine times, he's gone on to a hundred.
Across Test cricket, fewer than one in five ninety-plus scores stop short. For Pant, it's almost half.
Since 2002, only AB de Villiers and Alastair Cook have as many nineties, in more than twice as many Tests.
And you can see the nerves. Between 70 and 89, he scores at 105 runs per 100 balls. In the nineties, 73.
Nine Test hundreds, the most by any Indian wicketkeeper. Seven of them overseas.
Fix the nineties, and the record books might run out of room.
Beyond The Scoreboard.
